intro: Lazur is an AI assistant for Excel on Mac that works on top of the app you already have open. Hold ⌥ ⌘, ask where a button is or what a formula does, and it answers out loud. When you ask where something is, Lazur circles it on your screen. It does not click, edit cells, or change your workbook.
tldr: Ask 'where's conditional formatting?' and Lazur circles it on the Home tab.
Select a formula, hold ⌥ ⌘, and ask what it does. Lazur explains it piece by piece.
Ask 'walk me through a pivot table' and Lazur guides you one click at a time.
Hold fn to dictate text at the cursor. Lazur never clicks, edits, or changes your file.

blocks.text: What an AI assistant for Excel on Mac does

Lazur is a voice assistant that lives in the notch at the top of your Mac screen. You hold ⌥ ⌘, ask your question, and let go. Lazur looks at what is on screen, answers out loud, and points at things. It works in Excel, in Numbers, in a Google Sheets tab, and in any other Mac app you have open.

For a spreadsheet, that means four jobs. Lazur explains what is on screen or in a selected formula. It points at a button or menu and circles it. It walks you through a feature one click at a time, waiting for each click. It also drafts text and types it at the cursor when you ask. Lazur does not click for you, and it does not edit the workbook.
Nothing gets installed inside Excel. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app. You keep control of every cell, and you do every click that changes the file.

Microsoft 365 had about 89 million consumer subscribers as of July 2025, according to Office Watch, a secondary source. That was the last figure Microsoft published before it stopped reporting the number. Many of those subscribers open Excel on a Mac every day. Mac shortcuts use ⌘ instead of Ctrl, so generic Windows tips often miss.
The Excel problems people search for most

Most Excel help searches start with something broken. A 2022 survey of 500 people, run by Acuity Training and reported by Global Excel Summit, asked which Excel problems people hit most. Formulas that return errors such as #REF and #NUM came first. The article says that was almost twice as many complaints as the next problem.

Chart formatting came second. Formulas that return wrong or unexpected values came third. Getting a chart to show the correct data ranked sixth. The sections below follow the same order of problems, because that is the order people ask about them.

The same survey says 57% of people need help with Excel every week. That is a lot of small questions, asked in the middle of a task. Few people want to stop, open a browser, and dig through an old forum thread. That short gap is where a voice question fits.
Which Excel tasks send people looking for help

items: A formula shows #N/A, #REF, or #NUM. Start with the error section below.
A formula runs but returns a number that looks wrong. Ask what the formula does.
A chart looks wrong or shows the wrong data. Ask Lazur to point at the chart settings.
A feature is hidden on the ribbon. Ask where it is.
You need a pivot table, a drop-down list, or Data Validation. Ask for a walkthrough.

blocks.text: Sort your question into one of those five buckets before you speak. A question about one feature or one cell gets a sharper answer than a question about the whole file.
Ask where a feature is and Lazur circles it

The Mac ribbon looks like the Windows ribbon. Shortcuts use ⌘ instead of Ctrl, and some dialogs open in different places. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and say 'where's remove duplicates?' Lazur circles the button on the Data tab. Then it names what the button does, so you know you found the right one.

Use the feature name Excel uses. 'Where's the Format Painter?' gets a faster answer than 'how do I make it look nice?' The first question has one target. The second has many possible answers, and Lazur has to guess which one you mean.
Lazur can only circle what is on screen. If the tab you need is closed, open it first. If the ribbon is collapsed, the buttons are hidden, so expand the ribbon before you ask.

blocks.title: Collapsed ribbon
blocks.text: Press ⌘⌥R to expand or minimize the ribbon. Then hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask again. Lazur can only circle buttons it can see.
Ask what a formula does, piece by piece

Select a cell that holds a formula, hold ⌥ ⌘, and ask 'what does this formula do?' Lazur reads the formula from the formula bar and explains each part out loud. Try it on a common lookup like this one: `=IFERROR(VLOOKUP(A2,$E:$F,2,FALSE),"Not found")`

IFERROR is the outer wrapper. It checks the result of the VLOOKUP inside it. If the lookup fails, it shows Not found instead of an error. VLOOKUP looks for the value in A2 and searches the first column of columns E and F. The 2 tells it to return the value from the second column. FALSE asks for an exact match.

Follow up with a question. 'Why FALSE and not TRUE?' is a good one. TRUE allows approximate matches. Approximate matches can return a wrong row with no error at all. That is harder to spot than #N/A, which is why exact match is the safer default.
Ask about the parts you do not understand, one at a time. A long question about a whole sheet gets a vague answer. A single formula gets a clear one.

blocks.title: An explanation is not a test
blocks.text: Lazur can explain a formula. It cannot know your data is right. Check the result on one row where you already know the answer.
Fix #N/A, #REF, and #NUM errors in Excel on Mac

Each error points at a different cause. #N/A usually means a lookup found no match. #REF means a formula points at a cell that was deleted or moved. #NUM means a function received a number it cannot work with. Ask 'why is this showing #N/A?' and Lazur looks at the cell, then names the likely cause.

items: A name with a trailing space in one list but not the other. The lookup then returns #N/A. TRIM on the lookup value often fixes it.
A number stored as text. It looks like a number, but a lookup does not match it to a real number.
A range that broke after you deleted a row or column. That often shows up as #REF.
The square root of a negative number, which returns #NUM.
A lookup range that does not include the column holding the lookup value.

blocks.text: Work through the causes in that order. Check spaces first, then text numbers, then ranges. Each check takes seconds. The first two are the easiest to miss, so check them early.

A common mistake is pressing F9 and expecting a fix. F9 recalculates the workbook. It helps when results look stale. It does nothing for a formula with the wrong range. Use F9 when numbers look old. Use an explanation when numbers look wrong.
Walk through a pivot table one click at a time

Some tasks need several clicks in the right order. A pivot table, a drop-down list, and Data Validation are good examples. Ask Lazur to walk you through it. It circles the first button and waits. When you click, it names the next step. Your eyes stay on the sheet the whole time.

Here is how a pivot table walkthrough usually goes. Select your data with its header row. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and say 'walk me through a pivot table.' Lazur starts at the Insert tab and circles the PivotTable button. Then it names the fields for Rows, Columns, and Values. You choose the fields and do the dragging. The [pivot table guide](/how-to/make-a-pivot-table-in-excel) has the full menu path if you want it on paper.

items: Select the data, including the header row, as one block.
Ask for a walkthrough and wait for the first circle.
Click the circled button. Lazur then names the next step.
Drag the fields Lazur names into Rows, Columns, or Values.
Check one total against a number you already trust.

blocks.text: Edge case: blank header cells give a pivot table generic column names. Those names are hard to read later. Fill the headers first, then ask again. If your data sits in an Excel table, say so in your question, because the first steps change.
A drop-down list follows the same pattern. Ask for the walkthrough, then click the Data tab when Lazur circles it. Lazur waits at each step, so you can stop and check the sheet any time.
Dictate and draft text without leaving Excel

Hold fn to dictate. Speak, let go, and clean, formatted text lands at the cursor. That works in any app. Use it for a cell note, a comment, or the body of an email. Dictation is unlimited on both Lazur plans.

Drafting is a different job. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and say 'draft an email to Sam with these totals.' Lazur reads the totals on screen, drafts the text, and can type it at your cursor. Read every number before you send it.

Check the numbers carefully. A cell can display a rounded value while the full number sits behind it. The number format hides the decimals. A draft that copies the displayed figure can then disagree with the workbook.
Text you repeat is faster as a snippet. Add client names and product codes to your personal dictionary once, so dictation spells them right. Clipboard slots hold text you paste often.
Excel for Mac keyboard shortcuts that save clicks

Shortcuts still beat voice for moving around a big sheet. The table below comes from Microsoft's keyboard shortcut page. That page covers Excel for Microsoft 365, Excel 2024, and Excel 2021 on Mac. Keys can vary by keyboard and macOS version, so test each one once.

rows: Press Fn with the arrow key
If F9 does nothing, press Fn+F9
Recalculate every sheet in every open workbook
Use when several files look out of date
blocks.caption: Mac keys from Microsoft's Excel keyboard shortcuts page

blocks.text: If a function key does nothing, press Fn with it. You can also change the macOS setting that makes F1, F2, and the rest act as standard keys. That setting applies to the whole system, so it changes other apps too.
Some macOS shortcuts clash with Excel. Microsoft marks those conflicts with an asterisk. You can clear them in System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts.
Limits of a big workbook and what Lazur can see

Excel has large limits. One worksheet holds 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns. A single cell holds up to 32,767 characters. A column can be up to 255 characters wide. Microsoft's spec page does not list Mac differences, so read these as the general limits.

Lazur works from what is on screen. It reads the selected cell and the formula bar. It sees the rows you can see. A question about a row near the bottom of a long list needs you to scroll there first. Scroll to the row, hold ⌥ ⌘, then ask.

blocks.title: Screen, not file
blocks.text: Lazur sees a screen, not the whole file. Use it to find and explain things. Use Excel itself to filter, sort, and total the full data.
Excel for Mac versions and macOS requirements

Microsoft's Mac release notes list Excel 16.114.3, build 26102720, dated October 27, 2026. The entry reads Quality and performance improvements. A newer build may already be out. Check the notes before you rely on an exact menu position.
Updates need macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later. On older macOS, Office still runs, but it gets no updates, including security updates. Versions 16.78 and later need macOS 12 (Monterey) to install.

To see your Excel build, choose Excel > About Excel. To see your macOS version, choose Apple menu > About This Mac. Lazur runs on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.
A worked example: a total that does not match
Say a column of sales rows adds up to a number that does not match your bank report. This sequence works well with Lazur on screen. It takes a few minutes once you know the steps.

items: Select the total cell and ask 'what does this formula do?' Lazur explains the range it adds.
Ask 'why is this total different from the rows?' Lazur looks at the cells in the range and names what it sees.
Select a row that looks off and ask about its format. A text format can hide a number.
Press Shift+F9 to recalculate the active sheet if the totals look stale.
Fix the source cells, then ask Lazur to check the total again.

blocks.text: Two causes come up often. The first is text that looks like a number. SUM skips text values, so the total comes out low. The second is a range that stops one row short. Lazur points at the range inside the formula, so you can see where it ends.
Mistakes people make with an AI assistant in Excel

items: Asking about the wrong cell. Select the cell first, then hold ⌥ ⌘.
Trusting an explanation without testing it on one row you know.
Expecting Lazur to click. It points and waits. You do the clicking.
Forgetting that it looks only while you hold ⌥ ⌘.
Writing a summary from totals you have not checked.

blocks.text: Keep each question short. A short question gets a short, useful answer. A broad question about a whole workbook gets a vague one, because Lazur sees one screen at a time. Ask about one formula, one error, or one feature per turn.
Privacy for finance and client data

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your memory of what you asked and did stays on the Mac.

Client data needs more thought. Many firms set their own rules for AI tools and client files. Check your company's policy before you ask about a workbook with personal data in it. Lazur does not change that policy. That call belongs to you and your employer.

blocks.title: Close sensitive windows first
blocks.text: Lazur sees what is on screen while you hold the keys. Close sensitive tabs and windows before you ask about them.
How to start with Lazur in Excel

items: Download the Mac app from the [download page](/download) and open it once.
Open your workbook in Excel and select the cell you care about.
Hold ⌥ ⌘, ask what is on screen, and listen to the answer.
Try one point question and one walkthrough on the same sheet.
Check the [pricing page](/pricing) for trial details and plans.

blocks.text: The trial needs no credit card. It starts the first time you open the app. If your work centers on budgets and forecasts, the [financial analyst Excel page](/for/financial-analysts/excel) shows the kinds of questions that fit that work.

faq.question: Is Lazur an Excel add-in?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and nothing is installed inside Excel. Lazur looks at the screen only while you hold ⌥ ⌘.

faq.question: Can Lazur change my workbook for me?
faq.answer: No. It does not click buttons, edit cells, or operate Excel for you. It explains, points, and walks you through each step. It can draft text and type it at the cursor when you ask.

faq.question: Does it work with Numbers and Google Sheets?
faq.answer: Yes. It works with any Mac app you have open, including Numbers and Google Sheets in the browser. It is not a plugin for either one.

faq.question: Which Macs does Lazur run on?
faq.answer: Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned but not available. Microsoft's release notes say Office updates need macOS 14 or later.

faq.question: Does Lazur keep my spreadsheet data?
faq.answer: Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your memory of past questions stays on the Mac.

faq.question: Do the shortcuts on this page work in every Excel version?
faq.answer: Microsoft's shortcut page covers Excel for Microsoft 365, Excel 2024, and Excel 2021 for Mac. Older versions were not checked. Test a shortcut once before you rely on it.
